To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the current approach to dyskinesia is not ideal.

(1) dyskinesia should be considered as a noise that reduces the signal-to-noise-ratio in PD; (2) the goal of clinicians should not only be to reduce the amplitude of dyskineis, but also to improve the SNR by enhancing the motor repertoire of the patient; and (3) the current SNR approach can help clinicians to better assess the impact of their management strategy on the quality of the life of patients.
Dyskinesia, the major complication of levodopa (L-DOPA)-based therapies, is a factor in a SNR equation where the signal represents voluntary movement and the PD symptomatology, the noise.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the quality of life in patients with PD and with the health-care system in which they live.
the development and testing of a new paradigm for the assessment of the quality of life in PD patients.
the development of a new approach to the management of dyskinetic patients, which is based on the SNR equation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the goal of the treatment of PD should be to maintain or improve the motor repertoire of the patient and not to reduce the level of dyskinesias per se.
the goal of clinicians should not only be to reduce dyskinesia but also to improve the quality of life and the motor repertoire of PD patients.
the management of dyskinetic patients should be based on an SNR approach.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the SNR approach to the management of dyskinetic PD patients is a novel and potentially effective way of improving the quality of life for patients and their families, while also reducing the burden on the health-care delivery system.
dyskinesias can be considered as noise in a signal-to noise ratio (SNR).
clinicians should strive to maximize the SNR in their patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the SNR approach may be a more effective way to view the treatment of dyskinesias.
the goal of clinicians should not be simply to reduce the level of dyskinesias, but rather to improve SNR in PD patients, thus enhancing their ability to engage in activities of daily living.
dyskinesias can be managed in a more efficient way if they are not considered as a separate issue, but rather as part of the motor repertoire.
